issues.issue: The preamble describes the Trust as "successor to and representative of the estate of the Debtor", a phrase whose reach (which claims and whose claims pass to the Trust) is not fixed here. It also imports undefined capitalized terms from the Plan, leaving the definitional boundary uncertain.
The preamble incorporates Plan definitions wholesale while Section 9.8 makes the Plan control on inconsistency; a term used differently here and in the Plan would have to be reconciled.

The recital says the Trust is created solely on behalf of holders of allowed Class 2 claims, but operative Section 3.6 directs the Trustee to make distributions to holders of Class 1 claims and Section 1.2 refers to Class 3 holders. Recital and operative text point in different directions on who benefits.
The "sole purpose" recital (benefit of Class 2 holders only) cannot be squared with Section 3.6, which requires distributions to Class 1 claim holders out of proceeds of their collateral.

"each and every asset of the estate" is undefined at the margin — whether it captures causes of action that arguably belong to individual creditors rather than the estate is exactly the kind of question that decides a trustee's standing.

The transfer is stated to be "free and clear of any lien, claim or interest", which cannot be reconciled with Section 1.1(b) (assets transferred subject to listed liabilities) or Section 3.6 (distributions to Class 1 holders from proceeds of "the assets securing said claims").

This subsection transfers the Trust Assets "subject to the following liabilities", directly contradicting the immediately preceding Section 1.1(a), which transfers them "free and clear of any lien, claim or interest".

The Trustee's unilateral power to transfer "any and all assets of the Debtor or its estate" sits awkwardly with Section 1.1(a), under which every estate asset already vested in the Trustee on the Effective Date.

The reference to "the holders of allowed Class 3 claims" is a mechanical error: the same sentence and the rest of the instrument deal only with Class 2 (and, in Section 3.6, Class 1) holders. A reader cannot tell whether Class 3 holders were meant to be bound by the deemed-transfer treatment.
The Class 3 reference cannot be reconciled with Section 2.1, which makes holders of allowed Class 2 claims the only record holders of Liquidating Trust Interests, or with the Class 2-only recitals.

The mandatory duty to "use a custodian (such as a qualified bank or a company that is a member of a national securities exchange)" gives only illustrative examples, leaving who qualifies as a permissible custodian unfixed.
Section 2.1 limits record holders to holders of allowed Class 2 claims, which is in tension with Section 3.6's direction that distributions also be made to Class 1 claim holders.

The ban on "any steps, directly or indirectly, to facilitate the development of a secondary market" is a general prohibition followed by four specifics "without limitation"; its reach beyond the listed acts is undefined.
The grant that Interests "are transferable upon written notice" pulls against the same sentence's prohibition on facilitating transfers, and against Section 6.1's securities-law assumptions.

Section 2.3 says the Agreement grants "exclusive authority over administration of the Liquidating Trust to the Trustee", which is hard to square with Section 3.3(e), under which the Trustee is supervised by, reports to, and needs the approval of the Committee for dispositions of $5,000 or more.
"in an expeditious but orderly manner" and "not unduly prolong" are standards with no benchmark, and "or otherwise" opens the enumerated methods of liquidation.

Subsection (l) authorizes payment of "fees and reimburse the of expenses of any professionals or employees employed by PCCC" — "PCCC" is defined nowhere in the Agreement and the phrase is grammatically broken, so who may be paid is unascertainable.

The opening statement that nothing requires the Trustee to seek court approval, together with (x) (sell or transfer any Trust Assets "as the Trustee shall deem advisable") and (dd), collides with Section 3.3(e)'s requirement of Committee approval for dispositions of assets worth $5,000 or more.

"shall not take actions snconsistent with the Plan" contains an obvious misspelling, and "actions inconsistent with the orderly liquidation ... as are required by applicable law" is syntactically garbled about what applicable law requires.
The "[n]otwithstanding anything herein to the contrary" limitation must be reconciled with the sweeping authority granted in Sections 3.2 and 3.5.

The flat prohibition on any action resulting in Investment Company Act registration is in tension with Section 6.1, which contemplates the Trustee taking "any and all actions to comply with" Investment Company Act requirements if they apply.

This subsection limits the Trustee's compensation and expense rights "to the extent, and in the manner provided in, the Plan", while Section 4.7(a) lets the Trustee raise her own rates annually on ten days' notice "without approval of the Bankruptcy Court".

The carve-back — "the Trustee shall be entitled to take any other action with respect to such assets ... without obtaining approval of the Committee" — leaves "any other action" undefined against the specific list of sale, liquidation, abandonment and disposal, and "gross fair market value of $5,000 or more" does not say whether assets are valued singly or in the aggregate.

The Committee-approval requirement conflicts with Section 3.5, which lets the Trustee dispose of Trust Assets "without prior or further authorization", and with Section 2.3's grant of exclusive administrative authority to the Trustee.

The quorum definition overlaps at exactly three members: clause (1) makes three members a quorum while clause (2) requires all members when the number "is reduced to three or fewer", so a three-member Committee has two inconsistent quorum rules. The repeated "reasonable under the circumstances" standards for notice and for the email-approval period add no measurable boundary.

Bankruptcy Court resolution of Trustee/Committee disputes assumes a pending case, whereas Section 9.4 confers exclusive jurisdiction only "[f]or so long as the Chapter 11 Case may be pending" and says nothing about disputes afterwards.
A holder's access right is conditioned on it not being an "undue burden" and not "detrimental to the Liquidating Trust", vague standards the Trustee applies to requests directed at herself.
The duty to keep records sufficient for a "full and proper accounting" sits against Section 3.2, which says nothing in the Agreement requires the Trustee to file any accounting.

The authority to act over disposition of Trust Assets "without prior or further authorization" contradicts Section 3.3(e), which permits disposition of assets worth $5,000 or more only with Committee approval.
"within a reasonable time after liquidation of all assets" sets no ascertainable deadline for the mandatory distribution.

The direction to distribute to holders of Class 1 claims cannot be reconciled with the recitals and Sections 2.1 and 3.1, under which the Trust exists solely for holders of allowed Class 2 claims, nor with Section 1.1(a)'s "free and clear of any lien" transfer.

The parenthetical is broken — "(including the receipt ... by the Internal Revenue Service) upon audit if not contested by the Trustee)" has mismatched parentheses, so it is unclear what the adverse-determination carve-out attaches to.
This section is numbered 3.8, the same number as the preceding "Reporting by the Trustee" section, so cross-references to "Section 3.8" are indeterminate.

It assumes "proceeds of borrowings" exist, but no provision of the Agreement grants the Trustee power to borrow — Section 4.7(b) likewise assumes borrowing "in accordance with the terms of this Trust Agreement" that appear nowhere.

The closing words "except that the Trustee may deal with the Trust Assets as permitted by herein" are ungrammatical and circular, and appear to except the Trustee from the very fiduciary limitation the sentence imposes.

The power to prosecute claims "whether or not such suits are brought in the name of the Liquidating Trust, the Trustee, the Debtor, the estate or otherwise" leaves the class of claims the Trustee may sue on open-ended, and "reasonable business judgment" is unmeasured.

Section 4.2 duplicates Section 3.1's liquidation mandate in slightly different words (adding "transfer" and "reasonable business judgment"), so the two must be harmonised on the scope of the Trustee's liquidation power.

The final sentence — professionals' "determinations shall not result in the imposition of liability upon the Trustee" — protects the Trustee even where she does not consult, blurring the boundary of the advice-of-counsel safe harbour.
The mandatory indemnity here ('shall indemnify') is qualified by Section 4.3(f), which limits the Trustee's indemnification to amounts not covered by insurance, and by 4.3(d)'s repayment obligation.

The clawback of advanced expenses is imposed only on "the Trustee", although advances are made to the Trustee, the Committee and its members — by expressio unius the Committee keeps advances even if it acted in bad faith.
The insurance-first limitation applies only to "the Trustee", while Section 4.3(c) indemnifies the Committee, its members and professionals without that limitation.
Third parties may rely on the Trustee's authority without inquiry, which is hard to reconcile with Section 3.3(e)'s requirement of Committee approval for dispositions of $5,000 or more.

The opening sentence is garbled ("the Trustee, and the Trustee and shall be entitled to reimbursement"), and the closing sentence lets the Trustee "increase said compensation" annually with no cap, standard or consent requirement.

Self-help rate increases "without approval of the Bankruptcy Court" conflict with Section 3.3(d), which limits Trustee compensation "to the extent, and in the manner provided in, the Plan", and with Section 9.8's rule that the Plan controls.

The clause presupposes a power to "borrow funds ... in accordance with the terms of this Trust Agreement", but no provision of the Agreement (including the enumerated powers in Section 3.2) authorises borrowing.

The temporal phrase is broken — "while serving as Trustee under this Trust Agreement following the termination of this Trust Agreement or following the earlier of his or her removal or resignation" omits a conjunction, so it cannot be told whether the confidentiality duty survives termination or applies only while serving.

The final clause is circular: the Trustee serves until the proposed effective date unless the Court consents to an earlier effective date, "which shall be the date that appointment of a successor Trustee becomes effective" — the earlier date is thus defined by an event the Court may not have caused.
Section 5.1 has the Bankruptcy Court appoint the successor on resignation, while Section 5.2 gives replacement of a removed Trustee to the Committee in the first instance.

The section carefully defines "Cause" and confines Bankruptcy Court removal to it, then adds that "[t]he Trustee may be removed by the Committee without cause", leaving the enumerated Cause definition with no evident work to do.
Committee removal at will is difficult to square with Section 2.3's grant of exclusive administrative authority to the Trustee and with Section 3.3(e)'s narrowly drawn Committee approval right.
The acceptance instrument must be "in form satisfactory to the successor Trustee" — the successor approves the form of her own acceptance, which appears to be an error for the Court or predecessor.
